Five years ago a brownfield toll road in Latin America could offer an investor a double-digit return. Today the same asset struggles to promise nine percent, and the reason is not the traffic. It is demand. Pension funds and sovereign wealth funds have decided that operating assets, the ones that already earn money, are the safest way into the region, and so many of them are bidding for the same concessions that prices have gone up and returns have come down. Analysts call it yield compression. The result is a strange market. The safe assets are now expensive, and the greenfield projects that the region actually needs are still short of money. Several development banks are trying to close that gap with guarantees, so that a new project looks more like an old one to a cautious fund.

Let me be direct about how we look at your region. We do not start with the return. We start with what can go wrong, and in what order. Construction risk is the first thing we want somebody else to carry, which is why we like projects where a development bank has taken the early years. Currency is the second. Our investors are paid in dirhams and dollars, so if a deal does not come with a credible currency hedge, it does not reach our committee. The third is the contract itself. We have had concessions renegotiated in other markets after an election, and my board has a long memory. None of this means we will not come. It means the first deal has to be structured so carefully that we can defend it, and after that, capital deployment becomes much easier.
